Family Health

Skin abscesses: symptoms, treatment and follow-up

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A painful, warm lump containing pus may need more than an over-the-counter cream. Small boils sometimes settle, but a growing abscess, spreading inflammation or feeling unwell calls for medical assessment. Understanding the difference helps you use home care appropriately and get treatment before a local infection becomes more serious.

An abscess is a pocket of pus beneath the skin

A skin abscess is a collection of pus in the skin or the tissue just beneath it. It may look like a pimple at first, but is often deeper, larger and more painful. The surrounding skin can feel thickened, swollen or warm, and the centre may become softer as the collection develops.

Abscesses can occur almost anywhere, including the face, back, chest, lower abdomen and buttocks. Hair-bearing or friction-prone areas such as the armpits and groin are also common sites. A lump in these areas is not automatically an abscess: an inflamed cyst, swollen lymph node or another condition can look similar.

Boils, furuncles and carbuncles are related terms

A boil is also called a furuncle. It begins around an infected hair follicle and can extend into the surrounding tissue, forming a tender collection of pus. A carbuncle is a group of connected boils, sometimes with several points where pus drains. These names do not identify three unrelated illnesses.

Abscesses can also occur around a tooth or deeper in the body, including the abdomen, brain or tissues around the spine. Those require different assessment and treatment. Advice for a small skin boil should not be used to manage dental pain, neurological symptoms or a suspected internal infection.

Bacteria are common causes, but the circumstances matter

Bacteria can enter through a small cut, damaged skin or an inflamed hair follicle, even when no obvious injury is remembered. Staphylococcus aureus causes many skin abscesses; other bacteria, including streptococci, or a mixture of organisms can also be involved. Some staphylococci are resistant to commonly used antibiotics, which is one reason treatment cannot be chosen from appearance alone.

Less commonly, unusual bacteria such as mycobacteria, including tuberculosis, fungi or parasites can be associated with abscess-like lesions. Severe viral infection can also be part of an unusual clinical picture. These are specialist considerations, particularly when a lesion is persistent or the immune system is weakened, rather than the usual explanation for an ordinary boil.

Not every pus-like collection is an active bacterial infection. An inflamed ruptured cyst, reaction to injected material or an inflammatory skin condition can resemble an abscess. Repeatedly applying antibiotics without reconsidering the diagnosis may therefore miss the real problem.

Who may be more vulnerable

Skin problems such as eczema or acne can disrupt the skin barrier. Diabetes, immune-suppressing illness or treatment, and some metabolic health problems can also make infection more likely or harder to manage. Smoking is associated with some recurrent skin-infection patterns and can affect healing. None of these associations proves the cause of a particular lump.

Close contact with someone who has a draining staphylococcal infection, or contact with contaminated towels or equipment, can spread bacteria. Infection is not restricted to hospitals, although a recent hospital stay, operation or known resistant infection is relevant history. Tell the clinician about chemotherapy, an organ transplant, immune-suppressing medicines and previous cultures.

Recognise changes that need medical attention

A possible abscess may enlarge, become increasingly tender or throb, and leak fluid or pus. Redness can be difficult to see on darker skin, so warmth, swelling, pain and a change from the usual skin appearance are useful observations. Fever, chills or swollen nearby lymph nodes can accompany infection.

Seek prompt medical advice for a painful, hot or enlarging lump, spreading inflammation, fever or feeling unwell. An abscess on the face, especially near an eye, needs particular care. People with diabetes, a transplant or a weakened immune system should contact their care team early rather than trying home treatment first.

A lump that persists beyond two weeks, is hard and fixed, or repeatedly returns also needs assessment. The two-week point is not a waiting period when pain, fever or spread is already present. A breast lump needs its own clinical assessment, including during breastfeeding.

Know when infection may be becoming serious

Most localised infections can be treated, but some spread into surrounding skin or deeper tissue. Rare complications include bloodstream infection, sepsis, infection of bone called osteomyelitis, infection of the heart’s inner lining called endocarditis, and destruction of affected tissue. These are possible complications, not the expected outcome of every boil.

Sepsis is a dangerous whole-body response to infection that can damage organs; it is not simply another name for bacteria being present in a blood sample. Confusion, collapse, breathing difficulty, very rapid deterioration or feeling severely unwell requires emergency help. Rapidly spreading swelling or severe pain out of proportion to the visible skin changes also needs urgent assessment.

Examination guides the tests

A clinician will ask about the onset, previous episodes, injuries or ingrown hairs, medicines, medical conditions and associated symptoms. Examining the lump and nearby skin helps determine whether there is a pus collection, surrounding cellulitis or another explanation. Mention travel or unusual exposures if relevant.

A sample of pus can identify the organism and help choose an antibiotic, particularly for recurrent infection, treatment failure or other concerning circumstances. Ultrasound can show whether there is a drainable collection and how deep it extends when examination is uncertain. Some people need further imaging or a different type of sample.

Blood tests or blood cultures may be appropriate when someone is systemically unwell or has specific risk factors. A single normal test does not by itself rule out sepsis. The need for tests depends on the whole clinical picture; it is not true that every abscess requires only visual inspection and a swab.

Supportive care is for a small, uncomplicated boil

For a small boil without warning signs, a clean, comfortably warm compress can ease discomfort and encourage spontaneous drainage. One common approach is around ten minutes at a time, several times a day. Check the temperature carefully to avoid a burn. This is not a reason to delay care for a worsening or high-risk infection.

Do not squeeze, pierce or cut the lump yourself. If it opens, let it drain without force, gently clean the surrounding skin and cover it with a clean dressing. Wash your hands before and after wound care. A topical antibiotic cream cannot reliably reach a deep pocket of pus and should not be relied on as the main treatment.

Ask a pharmacist about suitable pain relief if needed, taking account of pregnancy, breastfeeding, other medicines and medical conditions. Do not place harsh disinfectants or household cleaning products inside a wound.

Drainage removes the collection

Many abscesses need incision and drainage by a trained clinician. The area is numbed, often with a local anaesthetic such as lidocaine, before an opening is made to release the pus. The clinician may clear separate pockets and clean or irrigate the space when appropriate. The technique depends on the location and extent.

A dressing is usually applied, and some wounds need packing or another method to keep drainage possible. Packing is not necessary for every uncomplicated abscess and can add discomfort. Ask exactly what has been placed in the wound, who should change or remove it, and when the next check is due.

Drainage often relieves pressure, but it does not guarantee that infection cannot return. Increasing pain, spreading redness, fever, continued heavy drainage or failure to improve should be reported. Follow the wound-care instructions rather than inserting new material or closing the opening yourself.

Antibiotics are selected for the individual infection

Antibiotics may be used alongside drainage according to the symptoms, surrounding infection, immune status, culture findings and local resistance patterns. Evidence in uncomplicated drained abscesses suggests that certain antibiotics provide a modest additional benefit, balanced against adverse effects such as diarrhoea or nausea. The decision should be discussed rather than treated as automatic prevention for every wound.

Medicines that may be considered in particular circumstances include clindamycin, doxycycline, trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole, cephalexin or dicloxacillin. They are not interchangeable. For example, cephalexin and dicloxacillin do not reliably treat MRSA, while the alternatives also have their own resistance and safety limitations.

Tell the prescriber about allergies, pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney problems and other medicines. Do not use leftover tablets or someone else’s prescription. Severe infection or important underlying illness may require hospital care and intravenous antibiotics as well as drainage. Report significant adverse effects and follow the prescribed plan.

Reduce spread and investigate repeated episodes

Keep wounds clean and covered, wash hands regularly, and avoid sharing towels, washcloths, razors, clothing or personal grooming items that contact the affected skin. Clean shared exercise equipment and other frequently touched surfaces according to the manufacturer’s instructions. A clean barrier between skin and shared surfaces can help.

Launder used towels, clothing and bedding with detergent on a setting suitable for the fabric and dry them thoroughly. Follow specific infection-control advice if provided. Bleach is not a universal requirement for every wash, should never be applied undiluted to skin, and must not be mixed with other cleaners. Supporting nutrition, diabetes care and smoking cessation can help overall health without guaranteeing prevention.

Abscesses can recur. Repeated lesions at the same site may prompt assessment for a retained foreign body, pilonidal disease or hidradenitis suppurativa. A clinician may sometimes recommend a targeted decolonisation regimen for recurrent staphylococcal infection. Do not start antiseptic body washes or nasal antibiotics indefinitely on your own; recurrence is a reason to look for the cause, not proof of poor hygiene.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Drainage is central to treating many pus collections; ultrasound and culture can help in selected cases.

Antibiotic decisions depend on the infection and the person, with modest benefits and adverse effects to discuss after uncomplicated drainage.

How BeMama can help

Keep the dressing instructions, next review date and medicine list together, and record any previous abscess locations and culture results.

When to seek help

Seek prompt care for a painful, hot or spreading lump, fever or immune suppression. Confusion, collapse, breathing difficulty or rapidly worsening severe pain requires emergency assessment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • A boil and a furuncle are the same type of follicle-related infection.
  • Do not squeeze, cut or pierce an abscess at home.
  • Creams cannot reliably treat a deep collection of pus.
  • Drainage, antibiotics and dressings are individual decisions.
  • Recurrent abscesses deserve investigation and do not prove poor hygiene.

Frequently asked questions

Can a skin abscess be treated like an ordinary pimple?

No. It can extend more deeply and may need drainage. Do not squeeze or pierce it, particularly if it is enlarging, painful or associated with illness.

Are a boil and a furuncle different conditions?

They are two names for a boil arising around a hair follicle. A carbuncle is a cluster of connected boils.

Should I wait two weeks before seeing a doctor?

No. Pain, heat, spreading inflammation, fever or high-risk medical conditions justify earlier assessment. Two weeks is not a safe waiting rule for a worsening infection.

Can I use a warm compress?

It can help a small uncomplicated boil. Use a clean cloth that is comfortably warm for about ten minutes, and do not let this delay care for warning signs.

Will an antibiotic cream reach the pus?

Not reliably when the collection is deep. A clinician can decide whether drainage or another treatment is required.

Does every drained abscess need packing and antibiotics?

No. Wound technique and antibiotic decisions depend on the case. Ask about benefits, adverse effects and the follow-up plan rather than assuming one approach fits everyone.

Are cephalexin and doxycycline interchangeable?

No. They cover different bacteria and have different safety considerations. The prescriber considers resistance, culture findings and your health history.

What if I am pregnant, breastfeeding or immunosuppressed?

Tell the treating team. These circumstances can change the urgency, antibiotic choice and follow-up, so use individual advice rather than someone else’s prescription.

Does successful drainage guarantee it will not return?

No. Recurrence is possible and may point to bacterial carriage, a foreign body or a condition such as hidradenitis suppurativa.

Do I need to disinfect everything with bleach?

No universal bleach routine is needed. Keep wounds covered, clean hands and shared surfaces, and launder items appropriately. Follow any targeted prevention plan from your clinician.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
